#6731. How Will Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Dress?

When Terence Young, the director of Dr. No, needed a suit for Sean Connery to wear for his debut as James Bond, he took him to see his personal Savile Row tailor, Anthony Sinclair.

“Connery’s suits were considered relatively contemporary, because Anthony always had a very soft shoulder on his suits,” explains Elliot Mason, the director of business at Anthony Sinclair, which is no longer located on Savile Row, but still makes classic British suiting. “Anthony liked to nip in the waist, so it gave that real hourglass silhouette to the suit, which really is quite timeless. And as was the trend at the time, the Connery suits all had a relatively high rise, double-pleated with English forward pleats, and most of his trousers had Daks button-tab adjusters on the side.”

Opting to dress James Bond in a Savile Row suit might seem like a no-brainer in hindsight, but the decision—and the cut of the suits themselves—still resonates more than 60 years later. Sinclair would make all of Connery’s suits during his nine-year run as James Bond, and his blend of classic British tailoring and of-the-moment influences would create a template for every Bond to come. With Robert Pattinson—a Dior ambassador and a guy with a reputation for adventurous style—chosen to take up the mantle in Bond 26, the question now becomes: what will he wear?

Tailor Anthony Sinclair fitting Sean Connery for one of the suits he wore in 1963’s From Russia With Love.

Ian Fleming, the author who created James Bond, spent a lot of time talking about what Agent 007 drank (Wolfschmidt Vodka) what he drove (Bentley convertibles, for the most part) and how he made his coffee (he was a dedicated pour-over guy), but, surprisingly, he never specified where the spy bought his clothes. As a result, for the last six decades, it’s been up to the directors and costume designers of the 25 previous films to create a new look for every successive Bond. In the Connery and Moore eras it was Savile Row suits. Timothy Dalton’s Bond wore Paul Smith. Brosnan was a bespoke Brioni guy, as was Daniel Craig, who also brought Tom Ford into the mix. At 6’1” to Craig’s 5’10”, with a leaner build, and a long track record of fashion-forward dressing, Pattinson has everything needed to reinvent Bond once again.

“I’m pretty sure we’re going to see something quite different from Pattinson's Bond,” says Matt Spaiser, the tailoring obsessive behind BondSuits.com and the author of From Tailors with Love: An Evolution of Menswear Through the Bond Films. “Pattinson is a different kind of actor, and he’s going to wear something that moves differently. Plus, he’s 18 years younger than Daniel Craig.”

The actor playing Bond has a major influence on how he dresses—Daniel Craig, an adventurous dresser himself, was very hands-on with the wardrobe in his films—but Pattinson’s ongoing contract with Dior could also factor in. “Some of his Dior looks look somewhat like James Bond—he wears a great tuxedo—but I don’t think it’s going to tell us what he’s going to wear as James Bond,” Spaiser says. “He’s worn suits from other brands in other roles—like in Tenet, he wasn’t wearing a Dior suit—so I don’t think he's necessarily obligated to be wearing Dior as James Bond.”

Daniel Craig, seen here in 2019 with then-Prince Charles on the set of No Time to Die, mainly sported sharp Tom Ford suiting in his later Bond films.

Another important factor that contributes to a new Bond’s look is what’s happening in fashion whenever the film eventually gets made. “One thing that we've seen throughout most of the Bond eras is that he dresses in suits that are fairly traditional, but there's always some nod to the era that they’re in,” says Spaiser. “Sometimes they lean a little more into fashion, like when Roger Moore was wearing flares. That was something that I think they couldn't avoid without making Bond look too old-fashioned at the time.”

Tone also plays an important role, and historically has ping-ponged between serious (Connery, Dalton, Craig) and more campy (Moore, Brosnan), but with Denis Villeneuve, the auteur behind Sicario, Blade Runner: 2049, and Dune in the director’s chair, the smart money isn’t on hovercraft gondolas and punny Bond girl names. A darker, more atmospheric milieu could make for an interesting complement to Pattinson’s taste for high-fashion.

If Mason were dressing Pattinson for the role, he says, he’d take a lead from his clientele, many of whom, like Bond, are well-heeled Londoners with a taste for expensive sports cars and well mixed cocktails. “The majority of our customers are reasonably conservative, and when it comes to fit, they’re sensitive to current trends,” Mason notes. As such, he’d opt for longer jackets, both single- and double-breasted, that are fuller through the body, and straight-leg pleated trousers. “It’s not that very, very slim fit that we'd seen for so many years, but it still needs to be refined,” he says. “I don’t think it would be appropriate to put him in wide-leg or baggy trousers. I just don't think it’s right for Bond.”

Robert Pattinson, the latest 007, has been the face of Dior’s menswear for over a decade.

Given the intense scrutiny on every relaunch of the Bond franchise, and the tendency of fans to get worked up online over perceived mishandling of a beloved character, Pattinson, Villeneuve, and the film’s yet-to-be-announced costume designers have little room for error. Go too conservative and they’ll be accused of playing it safe; make Bond into a fashion guy, and they’ll incur the wrath of the traditionalists.

“He needs to look current, but also timeless,” Spaiser says. “It’s a hard balance to find.”

#6730. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6728. The Best Foods To Buy At Costco In November

Our editors were blown away by one game-changing snack.

The holiday season is on the horizon, and Costco is celebrating with plenty of festive foods in every corner of the warehouse. Aside from the obligatory pumpkin pie, you can find party-approved appetizers, cozy bakery treats, and plenty of fall-forward snacks.

I spend all year keeping tabs on the latest and greatest products to hit Costco shelves. And as someone who writes about Costco for a living, I have a hot take: The food at the warehouse right now is the best it’s been all year.

Here’s what’s available this November—there are some treats you don’t want to miss.

The viral sensation has officially hit Costco. The Dot Cakes is a bakery on Long Island, New York, that exploded in popularity this summer thanks to its signature dessert: a single-serving cake in a cup covered in a generous layer of nonpareil sprinkles. Now, instead of waiting in long lines or trying to recreate it at home, Costco members can buy a six-pack of the real thing.

Each box includes both chocolate and vanilla cake, and both flavors are perfectly nostalgic. They taste like the best-ever birthday cake from your childhood, and the crunch of the sprinkles makes the experience even more fun.

It admittedly takes a lot for us to get excited about grapes—but these are worth the hype. Shine Muscat is a premium variety from Japan, famous for its large, sweet, seedless fruit. Many of the ones sold in the U.S. are imported from East Asia, including these Korean grapes now available at Costco.

I’ve had the pleasure of trying the grapes in smoothie form at a Costco food court in Seoul, but the real thing is even better. Our editors couldn’t stop eating them and compared the flavor to a plum or lychee. And at $10.99, they’re a fun upgrade that costs only a bit more than standard table grapes.

Want takeout flavors without takeout prices? Costco is now selling a noodle stir-fry kit that can feed the whole family for around $15. Each tray includes crispy breaded chicken pieces, yakisoba noodles, vegetables, and a sweet-and-savory sauce.

The meal is super easy to put together: Just crisp up the chicken in the oven or air fryer, then heat everything else in a pan. Costco is generous with the chicken and noodles, so the kit can provide at least four substantial servings. But if you need just one reason to add it to your cart, do it for the sauce. It’s just sweet enough with the slightest hint of spice.

Cabot Creamery has already combined its cheddar with popcorn, but this fall-forward version balances the sharp, salty flavor with a bit of sweetness. Each bag includes two types of popcorn: one seasoned with Cabot’s famous Seriously Sharp Cheddar and another with a maple syrup-flavored coating. Both are delicious on their own, but together? Magic happens.

The salty-sweet combo really works here, reminding us of those large popcorn tins with three different compartments, except everything’s mixed together. Your holiday movie marathon needs a bag of this.

Fans of the Kirkland Signature peanut butter pretzels need to grab this sweet treat. Jif’s Snappers combine mini pretzels, the brand’s creamy peanut butter, and a drizzle of milk chocolate. We love that there’s a higher peanut butter-to-pretzel ratio than with Kirkland Signature's version (and the PB is much softer). This snack has everything: It’s salty, sweet, crunchy, creamy, and impossible to put down.

Step aside, Snap, Crackle, and Pop. The brand Cloud 9 has upgraded the cereal-based sweet with flavors inspired by mango sticky rice. Each bar combines puffed rice with dried mango, coconut milk, and shredded coconut. And the Delish team agrees: This is arguably the best snack Costco has sold all year. It’s loaded with mango, lightly sweet, and full of interesting textures. Buy a bag and thank us later.

In just a few years, Swedish candy went from an uncommon novelty to a permanent fixture in the candy aisle. Now, Costco carries a Rolling Pin variety pack that includes sour gummies and foam candy (a Swedish staple with a marshmallow-like texture).

This 30-ounce bag features a wide variety of chewy textures and fruity flavors. If you’re just now dipping your toes into the world of Swedish candy, this is a great (and affordable) way to start.

Need fall breakfast inspo? Look no further. The newest addition to the Costco bakery is this maple pecan coffee cake, which is loaded with cream cheese, pecans, and maple flavor. The cake is topped with a crumbly pecan butter streusel and drizzled with the same icing Costco uses on its danishes.

Each coffee cake is $15, but it’s arguably worth much more given its sheer size. This thing is a behemoth—it’s tall and absolutely loaded with toppings. There’s also a thick layer of filling in the center that tastes nearly identical to pecan pie filling.

Baked brie is a party showstopper, and Costco now carries a kit with everything you need in one convenient package. Stonemill Kitchens’ kit includes puff pastry, a wheel of brie, chopped pecans, and caramel apple cranberry chutney. You’ll need to assemble it yourself before you throw it in the oven, but the instructions couldn’t be simpler. The puff pastry even comes with a sheet of parchment paper to protect your baking sheet!

And the results are straight-up showstopping. The melty, creamy brie pairs perfectly with the pastry and toppings. The chutney, despite the caramel in the name, isn’t too sweet—it adds just the right amount of festive holiday flavor. It’s so good that News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas even did a happy dance after taking a bite.

#6727. 15 Best Zip-Up Hoodies for Men 2026, According to GQ Editors

Surveying the best zip-up hoodies for men takes me back to my younger days as a hopelessly romantic high school kid. My formative years were marred by angst, soundtracked by pop punk, emo, and indie rock. The piece of clothing that got me through it all? A zip-up hoodie. It was core to the indie aesthetic, with every forlorn frontman sporting one over a thrashed band tee, skinny jeans, and shredded Chucks. But nostalgia never seems to stay in the past, especially when fashion is involved.

Gen-Z has revived every minute piece of 2000s pop culture, which means zip-up hoodies are back and have all but usurped the pullover hoodie as the sweat du jour. The zip-up is inherently versatile in both practical wear and sheer styling dexterity. With the flick of the zip, you can put your beloved Death Cab for Cutie tee on full display while letting your pits breathe, or keep it zipped up when it's just a bit too nippy out. To find the best zip-up hoodies on the market, I dusted off Transatlanticism and went on a deep dive. The good news is that the old classics are still good. The better news is that there's a lot of great competition to choose from.

Uniqlo’s no-nonsense clean aesthetic and low price point has made it a go-to for any menswear enjoyer looking for good style on a budget. While the brand excels at cashmere sweaters, T-shirts, and a slew of homerun collabs, the Japanese label’s sweats are criminally underrated. We’d go so far as to say that they should be talked in the same breath as brands like Champion and Sunspel. This zip up hoodie took us by surprise thanks to its comfy midweight, all-cotton fabric and solid construction. But the main selling point is the impeccable fit.

So many other brands cut their hoodies too long in the body and leave you looking like Jack Skellington’s pubescent brother. Uniqlo managed to cut its French terry hoodie to sit right at the hips which makes for a more classic and natural silhouette that’s neither lanky nor sloppy. Because of the fabric, the feel, and the overall fit, this is my favorite zip-up hoodie by a sizable margin. It’s my most-worn hoodie and has yet to show signs of any fraying.

Hoodies were originally meant for sportswear, as warm up gear before a grueling game of football. These days, they’re more often worn for lounging on the couch to watch the kickoff. And if you want to kick it in comfort while saving your pennies for booze and amuse bouche for the big game with the boys, the best budget zip up hoodie to buy is Hanes’ EcoSmart zip hoodie. The fit is spot on—relaxed, but not sloppy, comfy in the body and the sleeves without swallowing you like a sand pit.

The fit is impressive for the price, and the overall quality means you’re getting a little more than what you pay for. It’s not a hoodie that’ll last you for too long, but it is a good quality piece for just 15 bucks. And when other hoodies offer lesser quality and worse-fitting options for about the same price? The answer is clear.

It’s hard not to sing the praises of Reigning Champ, a brand that built its fleece empire on sweatpants and hoodies. The Canadian label’s flagship midweight terry fabric has drawn the attention of streetwear royalty and menswear buffs alike and its dedication to quality has elevated the humble hoodie to oxygen-deprived heights. We named Reigning Champ’s crewneck sweatshirt and pullover hoodie as among our favorites in their respective categories, and the same goes for its zip-up hooded sweatshirt. It’s made of the same 100% cotton French terry fabric as its superlative-earning brethren and is cut with high-quality flatlock stitching for a smooth, un-bulky feel.

I had high expectations for Reigning Champ, given my previous experience, and I’m not surprised at all with how nice this zip-up is. And while I'm partial to the standard fit, it’s also available in a slim fit version, too.

Hoodies live in a universe well beyond the sportswear world from which they originated. And while we still enjoy the OGs and the classics that made the hoodie a bona fide menswear must-have, we also love seeing all the ways the style has been pushed, tweaked, and freaked. Our Legacy's Level Hood has been a successful avenue for the Stockholm-based brand to explore the limits of the hoodie and this particular version strikes a delicate balance between the freaky and the fashion-curious. It's made of an English wool knit into an all-over ribbed texture for a throwback '90s feel. The cropped, boxy silhouette and elongated sleeves harken back to the grunge-y era, while the sultry dual-tone nightshade colorway throws you off in the best way possible.

Menswear influencers will be happy to regale you with their TedTalk on the golden ratio of clothing proportions. Essentially, that means your outfit should be divided into three equal sections where the top takes up one third of the outfit. Basically, your tops should be cropped and sit closer to your natural waist. Follow it up with some high-waisted pants with a wide silhouette and you’ve instantly garnered 300K views on TikTok (RIP). With so many indie brands and influencers scrambling to make their own versions of “the perfect cropped hoodie” you’re probably tired of wading through all the choices. Do yourself a favor and go to Abercrombie.

The Moose’s version is backed by actual trend forecasters, actual designers, and actual fit models. What does that mean, exactly? It means that its cropped zip hoodie fits really well and uses surprisingly beefy fabric. It was a revelation for me, too—Abercrombie wasn’t a name I associated with hoodies, but after I saw this in person, I had to readjust my menswear word cloud.

Some of the best zip-up hoodies for men are made by a brand you never see in brick and mortar stores. Camber has been crafting the most durable sweats for decades, right here in America and have been the shining example of the difference between good quality and great quality. Sure, you have to order through an old-school web 1.0 website and wait for several weeks to actually get your hoodie. But trust us when we say that the relatively minor inconvenience is completely worth it.

The heavyweight fleece is almost as thick as a leather jacket and can stand in as outerwear if you wanted it to. While other hoodies are washed to hell in giant industrial washing machines to reach a super soft texture by the time it gets to you, Camber’s actually require you to do the work yourself. It sort of feels like you’re being swaddled by an anaconda, which means if you’re a proponent of hard clothes like raw denim, you’ll like Camber’s hoodie a lot.

Cashmere zip hoodies, once the exclusive province of Silicon Valley unicorn founders and PJ-flying nepo babies, have been democratized, none better than Naadam's take. You know the brand for bringing thoughtful, sustainable cashmere pieces at “really, only that much?” prices. Its zip hoodie is as soft as it gets, with extra credit points awarded for coming in a classic fit (too many cashmere hoodies err on the side of slim) and six colors, including this decidedly handsome olive. Wear it on weekends, work-from-home Fridays, and long flights—even if it's just Economy+.

Shoutout to brother in arms Louis Cheslaw, GQ Recs contributor, whose writing for the newsletter Magasin put us on to young brand Cease. From seed to sewing, it's beefy 20-ounce cotton is fully American-made. Assembling the fabric vertically means the hoodie will shorten up to a slightly cropped, oversized fit. Act fast if you want some of the less-boring colors—they move fast.

We can’t deny Russell Athletic’s contributions to the hoodie space. And while its formula has changed over the years, the new hoodies are still pretty good for the price. The fabric is soft and lightweight, and it’s available in a rainbow of colorways. Plus, if you’re looking for a hoodie with a little more length, this is a great option.

Bold graphics aren’t usually deemed classics, but Gap’s retro-leaning collegiate-style block logo has staying power almost as much as the Levi’s red tab. Add to that a wonderfully fluffy midweight fleece material and a tailored straight fit and you’ve got something you’ll see on moodboards for generations to come.

Champion’s Reverse Weave fabric is iconic for its nearly shrink-proof quality and almost unsettlingly rough exterior. Flip it to the inside and you’ve got a luxuriously brushed interior that’ll have you feeling like you’re melting into a cloud. Heads-up that pricing varies kinda wildly by size on Amazon.

The secondhand market is chock full of navy-blue hoodies that have been sun-faded and beaten down with time. They'll cost you just as much as this Mfpen version, but will also fall apart faster than you can zip 'em up.

Les Tien's dedication to all things sweats results in a catalog of luxurious fleece and terry cloth with a modern approach. Featuring high-end Cobrax hardware, RiRi zippers, raw-edge hems and sleeves, and a heavyweight brushed fleece, no detail is phoned in.

The Real McCoy's is considered by many to be Americana repro wizards. This revival of an early 20th-Century hoodie is just one small piece of the brand's preservation prowess. It's made using beefy sinker-knit fleece, old-school Talon-style zippers, and vertical patch pockets.

A.Presse's chokehold on the menswear illuminati refuses to let up and it's pieces like this vintage-inspired hoodie that keep the pressure on. Based on very rare “after-hood parkas", this made-in-Japan hoodie features an idiosyncratic attached hood, super dense and lofty fleece, with artfully distressed details throughout.

Think of the zip-up as the pullover hoodie's elder brother, but with way more layering potential. In its most natural state, it can cuddle up to a matching set of sweatpants and a baggy tee with flair. (Top it off with a swanky necklace, crisp sneakers, and some stellar shades and you’re left with a fit on par with Shai Gilgeous-Alexander at his tunnel-trotting best.)

Unzipped and left open, it can also take on the role of a picture frame ready to display your sickest graphic tee—much like the cardigan, another treasure of 2000s fashion. Or make like a mid-Aughts garage band ironically donning corporate attire and wear your zip-up over a dress shirt and baggy tailored trousers, a high-minded fashion move with a jolt of kooky Scandinavian cool.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6726. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6725. Maple-Glazed Carrots

These maple-glazed carrots don’t hold back on the butter—or the brown sugar. Roasted with pure maple syrup and crushed red pepper flakes, they turn tender and glossy with a sweet-hot kick that complements everything from ham to lamb to green bean casserole.

The recipe began with Barbie—not the doll, but Andy Baraghani’s cousin’s former girlfriend. Her syrupy-sweet carrots became a fixture at family Christmas dinners. Some dishes are meant to last; some relationships aren’t.

For BA’s version, Andy traded the original’s hours-long cooking time for a hotter roast that gives the carrots browned edges and a buttery glaze. There’s no separate sauce to simmer: Everything goes straight onto a foil-lined (for easier cleanup) rimmed baking sheet, with regular tossing to coat the carrots in syrup as they cook. Finish with flaky salt for crunch and a welcome contrast to the sweetness.

No. This recipe calls for scrubbed, unpeeled carrots—give them a thorough cleaning and leave the skins on.

Keep the carrot pieces similar in thickness, halving or quartering larger ones lengthwise. Check the glaze each time you toss the carrots, especially once the edges begin browning: The sugars can darken quickly. Use tenderness and browned edges as your guide rather than waiting out the clock if the carrots are already done.

For a more savory version, try our Easy Roasted Carrots.

Place rack in middle of oven and preheat oven to 400°. Line a rimmed baking sheet with 3 sheets of foil (you’ll need it!). Cut 2 lb. medium carrots, tops trimmed to about ½", scrubbed, on a diagonal into 3" pieces (halved or quartered lengthwise if large).

Spread out carrots on foil. Evenly top with 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, ⅓ cup (packed; 70 g) light brown sugar, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Season with kosher salt and toss to combine.

Roast carrots, tossing every 20 minutes, until tender and browned around the edges, 50–60 minutes. Watch closely as the carrots begin to brown; the glaze can darken quickly. Transfer to a platter and drizzle with any remaining syrup. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt (if using).

Instead, we use a slow cooker that’ll help you whip up your stuffing alongside the stars of the show (roast turkey and pumpkin pie, obviously!). While you buzz around the kitchen, the slow cooker will cook your stuffing for you — resulting in a delicious Thanksgiving side dish waiting for you to serve up.

Arrange a rack in the center of the oven and preheat it to 350°. Spread bread on a baking sheet. Bake the bread, tossing it halfway through, until it is crispy and feels dry. The edges should just be starting to turn golden, which should take about 15 to 20 minutes. Meanwhile, melt butter in a large skillet over medium heat. When melted, add celery, onion, and herbs. Season with salt and pepper and cook until the onions are translucent, about 7 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool.

Grease your Crock-Pot bowl and add the toasted bread. Pour the vegetable mixture, eggs, broth, and parsley over the bread. Toss to combine and cover.

Cook on low for 3 to 4 hours, stirring after 2 hours have passed. Garnish with parsley before serving.

#6722. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6721. Pumpkin Pie Bars

Pumpkin pie bars are the easiest way to get the classic dessert on your Thanksgiving table. It requires no crust, chilling, or crimping. The crust is more similar to a shortbread crust, but the filling is just like the one you know and love. Looking for more ways to use all of that pumpkin you stocked up on? We have every single pumpkin puree recipe you'll ever need.

Arrange a rack in center of oven and preheat it to 350°. Grease a 12" x 17" baking sheet with cooking spray. In a large bowl, mix flour, butter, confectioners’ sugar, and salt until the mixture looks crumbly.

Press the dough evenly into prepared baking sheet, and bake until it is barely set and just starting to turn golden. This process should take about 20 minutes. In a large bowl, whisk pumpkin puree, cream, brown sugar, eggs, flour, cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, vanilla, and salt until smooth. Pour the filling over crust and bake until set and only slightly jiggly in the center. This should take about 40 minutes.

Let it cool completely before you cut the set mixture into squares.

Dollop with whipped topping and dust with cinnamon before serving. Enjoy!

Comprising everything from tees and tanks to shorts and jackets, YPB reflects Abercrombie’s ability to evolve while staying true to its heritage. The collection makes a convincing case for performance wear that goes beyond the usual sea of uninspired basics and head-to-toe Lycra. It’s also versatile enough to seamlessly move from a strenuous workout to the everyday wardrobe rotation. To put the collection through its paces, we’ve styled three looks that show just how far YPB can go.

This vintage-inspired muscle tank looks like some of the actual vintage tees that I’ve taken a pair of scissors to without a stranger’s set-in stains. I have a lot of hair that gets in my way so headwear is a must when working out. A bandana is a nice throwback to the classic bodybuilder era and unlike a hat, it does a better job at soaking up the sweat so it’s not dripping down my face.

The standout of this outfit is the shorts. Compression lined, they’re about as long as I’d go for shorts clocking in with a five-inch inseam. They have a discreet pocket in the liner to store my phone, and they're tight enough so my device doesn’t go flying out when I’m doing high knees. I’ve come to learn that recovery days are not only a blessing but a necessity. But they don’t necessarily mean you have to waste away on the couch all day. I can’t deny their comfort factor, and it’s hard to beat a sweater-and-shorts combo, an outfit beloved by my favorite A-listers.

The sweater was a quarter-zip with an elastic waistband for a more streamlined, tailored fit. And if I’m walking a little too briskly, the top easily comes off to reveal a staple graphic tee in my wardrobe.

Finally, I put on some pants! I don’t make it a habit to wear sweatpants out casually, but sometimes the weather calls for it. Hike ‘em up a bit and show off some crisp white socks, a style swerve I saw once and couldn’t help but copy.

The staple of this outfit is the heavyweight jacket. Its water-resistant lining keeps me dry when the meteorologists get the forecast wrong, and it’s lined to keep me warm as the days get shorter and the nights get longer. The two-way zipper also allows for some extra mobility, and it won’t bunch up when I sit down like so many other parkas.

#6719. Behind the Scenes of the Inaugural Bon Appétit LIVE

This past weekend the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in New York City opened its doors to the public for Bon Appétit Live, an immersive day of cooking demos and classes, talks with chefs and recipe experts, Test Kitchen tours, games, prizes, and plenty to eat and drink.

The day kicked off with a warm welcome from Bon Appétit’s editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, who exclaimed that “the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen is the heart of our brand.” Robinson also shared that Bon Appétit just launched a new cooking app containing tens of thousands of recipes from the Test Kitchen archives.

Guests fueled up with an impressive array of curated breakfast treats alongside refreshing beverages from S.Pellegrino, before moving on to interactive experiences.

In the first class of the day, baking novices and aficionados alike joined senior Test Kitchen editor and BA Bake Club expert Jesse Szewczyk in the Test Kitchen for Pie Crust Fundamentals, presented by East Fork. The hands-on class featured guest Keia Mastrianni, brand storyteller and “unofficial pie lady” of East Fork. Mastrianni proclaimed her enthusiasm for pie making: “I love preaching the gospel of pie. My favorite thing is teaching people to make pie dough with their hands.” Szewczyk agreed, emphasizing the tactile nature of the process: “It’s a very physical thing to do…a recipe can be written, but teaching someone to make pie dough requires demonstration.” Participants were in luck as Szewczyk and Mastrianni demonstrated a buttery pie crust fortified with cream cheese, a recipe ideal for Thanksgiving developed by former senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic. After Mastrianni shared crimping tips, participants made their own pie dough at stations throughout the kitchen, with Test Kitchen editors on hand to offer guidance. One participant, James, was particularly excited to be working with director of cooking Emma Laperruque. He enthused, “Before Emma’s and Chris [Morocco’s] recipes, I would burn water. [Bon Appétit] has made cooking really accessible, and I built a lot of confidence. I love the simplicity of Emma’s recipes…they are all so flavorful and so good.”

Each guest left ready for holiday baking season with new pie-making skills, and a ceramic pie dish from East Fork’s new bakeware collection, featuring clay and glaze made in-house with materials sourced in the Southeast. Before moving on to their next experience, Mastrianni encouraged everyone to keep honing their skills, emphasizing, “Practice makes pie. Progress, not perfection.”

Meanwhile, in the neighboring Demo Kitchen, a Pasta Boot Camp was underway with Bon Appétit senior cooking editor Kelsey Jane Youngman and chef Stefano Secchi. Secchi, chef and partner of New York City’s Rezdôra (recipient of one Michelin star) and Massara, honed his craft in Modena, Italy, under legendary chef Massimo Bottura.

After walking guests through the fundamentals of making and shaping fresh pasta by hand, Secchi demonstrated a filled ravioli dish aptly named Holiday in Parma. Made with 00 flour and egg dough, the ravioli was piped with a chestnut and Parmesan filling and served with a rich reduction of chicken broth, butter, and saba (a traditional Italian syrup made from slowly simmered grape must).

While guests savored their pasta in the Demo Kitchen, a lively panel discussion was underway on the 34th floor. Moderated by editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, the Bringing Culture to Cooking panel featured chefs Fariyal Abdullahi (executive chef, Hav & Mar, NYC), Nicholas Bazik (chef and owner, Provenance, Philadelphia, a Bon Appétit Best New Restaurant of 2025), and Vijay Kumar (executive chef and partner, Semma, NYC, a Best New Restaurant of 2022). The conversation explored how culture, identity, and personal experience inform each chef’s cooking. The chefs shared some of their favorite home-cooking ingredients, such as Chef Bazik’s fermented lime juice, a versatile seasoning made by combining fresh lime juice with salt at a 2% ratio by weight. Chef Abdullahi championed berbere, the Ethiopian spice blend she likened to “Ethiopian salt” for its ubiquity in the country’s cooking. Abdullahi cautioned that store-bought blends are convenient but not necessarily of the highest-possible quality. “You should make it at home!” she encouraged.

Back in the Test Kitchen, Visit Maine hosted Lobster 101, a hands-on lobster class and oyster tasting with Bon Appétit’s manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Each participant received a whole, steamed Maine lobster and the ingredients and tools needed to transform it into a creamy, decadent lobster dip. Under Westerfield’s guidance, the class learned how to break down their lobsters, extract the meat, and assemble a dip made with cream cheese, mayonnaise, celery, chives, and lemon juice. The approachable demonstration demystified the process and showed guests how easily they could prepare a luxurious appetizer at home, just in time for the holidays.

Participants worked with hard-shell lobsters, but Tripp encouraged them to visit Maine and sample both hard-shell and soft-shell varieties. She explained that soft-shell lobsters, typically in season from July through August, have a sweeter, more tender meat. The two are actually the same animal at different stages of its molting cycle: a soft-shell lobster has recently shed its old shell, leaving a newer, more pliable one that is easier to crack. The class concluded with a tasting of Aphrodite Oysters, grown in the waters off South Thomaston, Maine. The medium-size oysters were briny and subtly sweet, reflecting the cold, brackish waters of the Lower Weskeag River where they were grown. A small squeeze of lemon was all that was needed to enhance their flavor as guests tilted their heads back, slurped, and allowed themselves to be transported to the rugged coast of Maine.

Meanwhile, in the Demo Kitchen, Bon Appétit director of culture Joseph Hernandez was joined by Matt Conroy, chef at Washington, DC’s Maison Bar à Vins, for a live cooking demonstration of one of Chef Conroy’s favorite dishes. Named one of Bon Appétit’s Best New Restaurants of 2026, the restaurant pairs French-inspired cooking with an eclectic wine list and seasonal cocktails. Chef Conroy prepared a new fall salad made of chicory, pear, and smoked blue cheese, finished with a Banyuls vinaigrette.

In the cafeteria, guests gathered for a live version of the Dear Bon Appétit advice column. Bon Appétit director of cooking Emma Laperruque presented questions about home cooking and holiday entertaining to chef Amanda Freitag. One attendee asked Freitag how to handle undercooked turkey legs and thighs each year. Freitag recommended removing the legs and cooking them separately, as in this BA recipe for Gravy-Braised Turkey from Jesse Szewczyk.

Next, food stylist Thu Buser showcased her exceptional culinary artistry by decorating an elaborate “snake cake” with vibrant green swirls and flowers. Then, a break for lunch with BA’s Best Mozzarella Sticks, a variety of salads and skewers, hot honey salmon, smoothies, and a cranberry maple mule.

While attendees grazed and mingled, Jamila Robinson joined legendary chef and restaurateur Marcus Samuelsson to discuss Back to Green: Rediscovering a World of Delicious, Healthy Eating, his new global plant-forward cookbook coauthored by Robinson. Samuelsson captured the atmosphere of the event, remarking, “What a party we are having here…the energy is amazing!”

The final demonstration of the day featured Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote presented by Visit Maine with Jesse Szewczyk and Ron Howard of Brodis Blueberries. Featuring a recipe from Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firsker, the shortcakes showcased farm-fresh wild blueberries grown on a ninth-generation family farm. As Szewczyk prepared the recipe, Howard discussed the importance of wild blueberries to Maine’s agricultural heritage. A native crop, they can be traced back to the end of the last Ice Age, predating lobster as a symbol of the state. “Everyone should think of wild blueberries as the ultimate Maine crop,” Howard explained. After tasting the shortcakes, attendees would be hard-pressed to disagree. Szewczyk noted that compared with conventional blueberries, the wild blueberries produced a more saturated color and tasted more distinctly of blueberry.

The day ended on a sweet note with pastry chef Eunji Lee, winner of North America’s Best Pastry Chef Award from The 50. Attendees had a chance to meet Lee and sample pastries from Lysée, her pastry boutique influenced by Korean and French culture and inspired by New York City.

Bon Appétit Live brought together chefs, culinary personalities, and food editors for a day of conversations, cooking, tasting, and learning. Attendees experienced the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen firsthand, learned directly from chefs and editors, and engaged with the people and products behind the food. As editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson said, “Food is always an invitation…we are so happy to give everyone access to the same experiences we have.”

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Company, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

#6717. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6714. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6712. Gordon Ramsay’s Routine for a Six-Pack at 60 Includes Daily Crunches and Red-Light Therapy

Gordon Ramsay has earned 17 Michelin stars throughout his career and still oversees nearly 100 restaurants. He also fronts prime-time TV franchises on both sides of the Atlantic and holds a couple of casual Guinness World Records (call him if you need to fillet a 10-pound fish in 1 minute five seconds).

This is a man who’s never met a goalpost he didn’t want to surpass. So it wasn’t entirely surprising when he posted a bare-chested shot of his six-pack to the grid earlier this month. What generated headlines was the occasion: his 60th birthday. “Gordon Ramsay thirst trap was not on my bingo card,” reads one comment. “My wife is on this app sir,” reads another.

At home in London, he shows me the Insights section on his Instagram account, which reveals the photo has gotten over 62 million impressions. “It’s very strange,” he says. “I’ve had a lot of ribbing from my eldest daughter, Megan. She’s a police officer. She was like, ‘Dad, how can you do that to me?’ All her senior sergeants and officers were laughing and telling her to tell me they’re going for a run. They’re in their early 40s. And then my Royal Marines Commando son just sent me a message with: ‘WTF dad, what are you doing?’”

Ramsay has been a pretty active guy for a while now, despite working in an industry typically associated with chaotic diets and zero time for exercise. He was a youth soccer player back in the day, before becoming a chef and then, in his 40s, going from weighing 252 pounds to competing in marathons and Ironmans.

All very impressive, but it’s even rarer to be this chiseled in your 60s (maintaining a low body fat percentage becomes harder as your testosterone and growth hormone production slows down). Read on to learn more about his preferred forms of cardio, his favorite pre-workout treat, and why he's established a daily cryotherapy routine. “I call it my freezer,” he says.

“15 minutes a day. It starts off with a quick two-minute stretch and 100 sit-ups every morning. Precore lifestyle is my ab cruncher thing—these things are fucking amazing, by the way. If I miss a day, then I have to punish it and do double the next day.”

“It’s not physically hard with big weights. These are 25 pounds. I’ll do a strength class once a week, 45 minutes. That’s it. Occasional push-ups and squats. No personal trainer.”

“What’s helped tremendously, with no impact on any of the joints, is a lot of swimming. So I have an injury in my patella, my right knee, currently. So I just increased the swimming because that’s the only sport that can use every muscle in your body with zero impact. But cardio is off the charts.”

“I have a Zwift bike, so I jump on that for 45 minutes. There’s no impact on that. I’ll do that Monday, Wednesday, Friday and gear up for 90 minutes on a Sunday. If I wasn’t injured, I’d be doing three 5K runs again, Monday, Wednesday, Friday, 20-minute runs. I’ve got my 5K back down to 21 minutes. The dream is under 20. I was running at 19 and a half back in July. A 5K run is easy to do in the morning before work, it’s done within half an hour. Once I do that, I can gear up for either a two-hour bike on a Sunday or a 90-minute run. I alternate. So, one Sunday’s run, one Sunday’s bike.”

“10 years ago, I ruptured my Achilles. I invested in an AlterG, a beautiful running machine that takes your weight, so you get all the cardio you want and less impact on the joint.”

“From the chef’s perspective, I call it my freezer. It’s the cryochamber. I do two sets of three minutes every morning. I try to go seven days a week in that thing, straight after [working out]. That is incredible. That’ll get up to like minus 160. For six minutes.”

“I’ve invested in a tiny little red-light therapy sauna outside in the garden, and it seats two of you, and so [I’ll do] half an hour of that, every other day. This doesn’t need to be done every day. Three times a week’s fine. So when I’m not running, the other day I’ll sit in that red-light therapy and spend 20 minutes, 30 minutes in there, which is brilliant.”

“The older you get, the more you have to stretch. I use a lot of bands. And so after sitting and stretching, I had those incredible bands where you lift your feet up and pull and stretch. 5 minutes is always a nice stretch before you [work out] and then 10 minutes stretch after that. I’ve never been to a yoga class in my life.”

“I’m big on oatmeal for breakfast, Monday to Friday. I indulge Saturday, Sunday. I will do [oatmeal with] blueberry compote, caramelized banana for my potassium, and then fresh blueberries on top with some—it sounds weird, but it’s delicious—hot honey.”

“I have my friends at Precision. I’ll do one of their gels before I start that 5K, a protein gel, 30 grams, and then that sees me through the whole 45-minute routine. Coffee is just a full-fat, flat white, extra hot. Extra hot means I can sip it slowly. I cut out a lot of dairy, a lot of butter, a lot of cream. And so that treat in the morning with a flat white is that sort of, ‘I’ve earned this shit.’”

“I don’t overstress on that because I stay fit. I monitor what I eat, but if anything, I’ll do smaller portions now. I’ll involve a lot of spinach, involve a lot of salmon, chicken, especially thighs. We’re just smart with less cream, less butter intake. And then when we travel, we just keep it light.”

“I have a red wine with dinner, Californian, something light, something delicious. In 20, 30 years running restaurants, I’ve never gone around the room holding a glass of wine, holding a glass of champagne, sitting down, drinking with customers. Again, discipline.”

“Just a couple of spoons of creatine, five mornings a week. A little scoop in my water.”

“One thing I’ve learned in my 50s and my 60s—everyone said the older you get, the less you sleep. I think it’s the other way around. I like to be in bed by 11, and I’m up at 6. My Oura ring for me has become my best mate, because it just gives me the proper day-by-day indication and then keeps you on track for sleep.”

“Sign up for something. Have a target because that gets you out of bed, with a bigger, incentivized plan. I need that target twice a year, every six months. And I’ve done that since my 40th birthday. Whether it’s half an Ironman, whether it’s a marathon, half a marathon, I’ve always got something to focus on.”

“No, no, no, no, no, no. Definitely not. No. I mean, no. My meditation is Kitchen fucking Nightmares. Dealing with some of those contributors on there and having to sit with them and talk with them. But no, not very good at sitting still.”

#6711. These Cozy Casseroles Are Perfect For Feeding A Crowd This Holiday (And Beyond!)

Casseroles remind me of cuddling up at home by the fire with my loved ones and digging into the tastiest dishes. They're also some of the easiest recipes to throw together in no time, and are the best for serving a holiday crowd. What else could you want? Now that we're firmly in the cold season, I can't stop craving them, so obviously, I turn to my favorite Delish recipes to make it happen. This holiday season, make sure to try out these 12 casserole recipes for some of the best bites you'll have all season. We have some classics, like a comforting chicken and rice casserole that'll have you dreaming of home, alongside more inventive and mouthwatering dishes like our French onion croissant strata.

There are few pairings as classic as meatloaf and mashed potatoes, but this casserole is anything but basic. Take your side of mashed potatoes, stack it on top of your meatloaf, and load it up with all of your favorite baked potato toppings. You’ll have an indulgent, craveable casserole that turns into the best leftovers—if you have any.

When you’re hungry for something that’s comforting, cozy, and a little luxe feeling too, chicken Marsala is a truly excellent option. The pan sauce has plenty of mushrooms, fortified Marsala wine, and a splash of cream, because why not? It’s a fantastic dinner, easy enough for a weeknight and special enough for date night.

A breakfast strata is one of our go-tos when we want a hearty, shareable brunch dish, but it’s hard to put into words how good this French onion croissant strata is. It takes a few extra minutes to deeply caramelize the onions, but the extra flavor and richness make a HUGE difference.

Chicken soup is a comfort food icon, good for the soul and the stomach, and there are a world’s worth of chicken soup recipes to choose from. Take chicken, egg noodles, some veggies, and a creamy sauce and bake them into a hearty casserole? You have a hearty dinner that leads to full bellies and happy hearts.

This slow-cooker casserole, featuring potatoes, beans, corn, and lots of cheese, is hearty, packed with flavor, and sure to make repeat appearances on your grub rotation all fall long.

Chicken and broccoli casserole is a meal that most people at Team Delish grew up eating, and this recipe is guaranteed to make you feel like a kid again. This creamy, cheesy, Ritz cracker-topped casserole is packed with chicken, rice, and freshly blanched broccoli with the quintessential cream of mushroom soup.

When it comes to this casserole, think breakfast strata with buttery, caramelized apples, and lots of sharp cheddar. If you’re in need of a quick fall-forward recipe to throw together for a weekend brunch, you can easily turn to this one.

When we need a direct flight to a quick and easy dinner destination, we turn to two trusty options: a casserole or a chicken dinner. This chicken and rice casserole is the best of both worlds. It requires minimal cleanup, and the hands-on cooking time is only 20 minutes. The rest of the time, you can just lounge in your living room while this whips itself up.

When the weather gets cold, your dinner making-mojo is low, or when comfort food is just what’s on the menu, you need a casserole. Even though we have loved so many other casseroles before, there's always room in my baking dish for one more. And if that casserole is easy, creamy, chicken-y, and cheesy? With a crunchy topping? Our oven is already preheating.

Watch out, classic green bean casserole, gnocchi has entered the holiday menu. We took the classic recipe and added gnocchi for a dish that's infinitely better than the sum of its parts. Blanched fresh green beans and buttery sliced mushrooms, onions, and garlic get tossed with a creamy béchamel sauce and pillowy gnocchi, then baked until bubbly.

This enchilada casserole is what weeknight dinner dreams are made of. Classic chicken enchiladas are a fan-favorite meal, but they can be kind of tedious to prepare when you're low on energy (all that rolling, right?). In this recipe, you just layer all your components in a casserole dish, bake until melty and saucy, add your desired toppings, and serve!

In our book, it doesn't get more comforting than shepherd's pie. Because this meat and potatoes dish is such a classic, we spent a while perfecting the comfort food staple—your weeknights should be as cozy as possible.

#6710. 5 Fall/Winter 2026 Wedding Guest Dress Trends You Can Still Shop

When it comes to styling, take a cue from Pieter Mulier’s Alaïa, where velvet gowns were paired with barely-there shoes and luminous, glowing skin. Jewelry, if any, should be kept to a minimum: A single, discreet earring is all the embellishment you need when the dress is this rich.

If velvet brought the opulence this season, fringe supplied the theatrics. Leave any bohemian preconceptions at the door: This season, the embellishment took on a decidedly more sophisticated character. Gabriela Hearst, Ulla Johnson, Akris, and Altuzarra each offered their own interpretation, from fluid strands tracing the contours of sleek evening gowns to exuberant cascades that transformed minimalist silhouettes into something way more fun. These are dresses best-suited to cocktail receptions and formal RSVPs, where a little theatricality is always welcome.

#6709. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6708. 31 Cranberry Recipes for Thanksgiving and Beyond

Look for firm, glossy cranberries and discard any that are soft, shriveled, or bruised. A few pale pink berries are nothing to worry about.

Keep unwashed cranberries in their original bag in the refrigerator for up to four weeks, though they’re best used sooner. To stock up, freeze them in their original packaging or spread clean thoroughly dried berries on a baking sheet until frozen, then transfer to a freezer bag. They’ll keep their quality for up to a year. Many cooked cranberry recipes work with frozen berries straight from the freezer; check the recipe before thawing.

That vivid magenta filling is no food-coloring trick: Cranberries and plenty of lime give the curd its electric hue and tang. Let the pie set overnight, then pile on billowy meringue and break out the kitchen torch.

A 12-oz. bag of cranberries, sugar, orange zest, and about 10 minutes at the stove are all you need for this tangy Thanksgiving essential. Make it up to five days ahead and save any leftovers for turkey-cranberry sliders.

Layers of tender buttermilk cake, tart cranberry jam, and silky white chocolate frosting make an excellent argument for serving cake on Thanksgiving. The sugared cranberries on top are like little sour candies.

Imagine Key lime pie dressed for the holidays. The punchy cranberry-lime curd meets a crisp press-in crust made with gingersnaps and pecans. A generous dollop of whipped cream rounds out the tartness.

Here’s a reason to keep canned cranberry sauce around after Thanksgiving. Jellied sauce melts into a glossy, sweet-and-sour glaze that coats chicken and green beans. Think orange chicken, with a cranberry twist.

Cranberries turn this classic upside-down apple tart a beautiful rosy pink while cutting through its buttery sweetness. Homemade rough puff pastry supplies the flaky base; vanilla ice cream is very much encouraged.

Canned whole-berry cranberry sauce becomes a punchy dressing for pleasantly bitter endive and frisée. Add crunchy candied pecans and salty Manchego, and suddenly cranberry sauce is doing salad duty.

Two layers of buttery, crumbly walnut crust surround a tart cranberry filling in this striking take on a Linzer torte. Save it for a holiday dessert table—or any occasion that calls for something special.

Dress crisp-bottomed Persian rice with dried cranberries, saffron, and fragrant herbs. The berries plump in ghee alongside rosemary, sage, and thyme, adding little pops of sweetness against the savory rice.

If the wobble is the best part of canned cranberry sauce for you, this homemade version delivers. It’s sliceable, deeply fruity, and subtly fragrant with cardamom and bay leaves. Bring on the ridges.

Roasted brussels sprouts get a lively companion in cranberry mostarda, a sweet-tart condiment with mustard seeds, prunes, and a little brandy. Make extra mostarda: It belongs on more than just sprouts.

A warm cranberry-apple topping brings plenty of tart fruit flavor to this crowd-friendly baked oatmeal. It’s a welcome breakfast when the house is full and everyone seems to wake up hungry at once.

Rum, hard cider, cranberry juice, ginger ale, and lime make a lively batch cocktail. Cranberry-studded ice cubes do double duty, keeping glasses cold and making the punch look party-ready.

Jalapeño and lime give classic cranberry sauce a bright, spicy kick. It’s especially good alongside roasted meats or piled onto a leftover turkey sandwich when you want something with a little heat.

Forget the giant roast bird for a minute. These tender, gravy-coated turkey meatballs come with a cranberry-orange marmalade jam that stands in for traditional lingonberries. A heap of mashed potatoes completes the picture.

Fresh ginger gives this cranberry relish some zip, while golden raisins and allspice round out its tartness. Spoon it onto a cheese board or save the leftovers for French toast the next morning.

Herbs in the dredge give this crunchy fried chicken Thanksgiving energy, but the quick cranberry-mustard dipping sauce is the real holiday flourish. It’s a compelling alternative to roasting an entire turkey.

Homemade cranberry-thyme syrup, Campari, and Champagne make a sparkling cocktail that’s fruity, pleasantly bitter, and dressed for a party. Make the syrup up to two weeks ahead; the drinks come together in minutes.

Boxed stuffing mix gets a serious upgrade with aromatic vegetables, dried cranberries, and the savory drippings from crisp-skinned chicken thighs. It’s Thanksgiving-adjacent comfort food, made in one skillet any night of the week.

Roasted sweet potatoes and delicata squash get a glossy, sweet-and-sour cranberry sauce made with red wine vinegar and thyme. Make extra: The agrodolce is just as good spooned over Thanksgiving turkey.

Whole orange and a cinnamon stick give this chunky cranberry sauce its fragrant warmth. Blanching the chopped orange first keeps bitterness in check, while a little butter softens the berries’ sharp edge.

A buttery, lemony custard studded with tart cranberries gives this Southern classic a holiday spin. The berries stay mostly intact, offering juicy little bursts of tartness against the rich filling.

Dried figs bring earthy sweetness to this bold cranberry chutney, while ginger, vinegar, and whole grain mustard keep it lively. It’s the sort of condiment you’ll want beside roast pork as much as turkey.

Dorie Greenspan’s warmly spiced Bundt packs in fresh and dried cranberries, toasted almonds, and a little five-spice powder. Greek yogurt keeps the cake rich; orange icing supplies the finishing flourish.

Baker Amanda Mack tucks a tart cranberry-orange filling into exceptionally flaky buttermilk pastry for individual pies. They’re a thoughtful addition to a dessert spread where everyone wants to try a little of everything.

No simmering required for this bright, crunchy cranberry relish. Walnuts, shallot, mustard seeds, and Fresno chile give it plenty of texture and bite—a particularly good counterpoint to rich holiday mains.

Homemade cranberry-orange jam gives this tequila cocktail its fruity punch. Lime juice keeps it lively, while a sugar-salt-and-five-spice rim makes each glass taste decidedly more festive than a typical margarita.

Chopped fresh cranberries bring little bursts of tartness to an otherwise classic cheddar grilled cheese. A swipe of Dijon mustard ties the flavors together. Sometimes the best cranberry recipe is also lunch.

Have part of a bag left over? These ideas from the BA archives put even a small quantity to good use.

#6707. A Brief Guide to Grand Theft Auto VI’s Nike Sneaker Dupes

GTA 6 is finally out, which means we’ve got some in-game sneaker shopping to do. We’d already spotted Air Force 1 dupes in the trailers, but now that we can finally play the long-awaited masterpiece itself, we’re taking a closer look at what else is on the shelves. There are tons of different sneaker stores sprinkled throughout the game, and Eris—Rockstar’s fictional answer to Nike—has given us a lot to work through.

Even the name is a joke. Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory, while Eris is the goddess of strife and discord—an appropriate choice for kicks you might buy with money from an armed robbery. The Swoosh has been replaced with a pointier, upside-down logo, and plenty of the sneakers baring the mark are instantly recognizable.

The Eris Rise Low is the obvious starting point. It’s the game’s AF1 equivalent, complete with the familiar paneled upper, perforated toebox, and a big, beefy sole underfoot. The Eris Strife 360, meanwhile, looks straight out of the Air Max 97 catalog. There’s the rippling upper, rounded toe, and long cushioning window underneath. Designed by Christian Tresser and released in 1997, the IRL sneaker’s silhouette took inspiration from water ripples, while the OG “Silver Bullet” finish drew on mountain bike components. Eris keeps enough of that shape for you to be able to spot it from across the shop.

Some versions get even more specific. There’s a white-and-orange Strife 360, for example, with oversized branding, contrasting lace loops, and printed side text that recalls Off-White’s own Air Max 97s. It isn’t a straight one-to-one recreation, but the reference feels pretty clear. An apparent take on the Off-White Air Force 1 Mid also appeared in the teasers. Someone at Rockstar is clearly a fan of Virgil Abloh’s work.

Then there’s the Eris Strife 90, with pairs that borrow heavily from the Air Max 90 “Infrared.” The bright red accents and sharp, aggressive lines are all there, with one colorway even adding black scribbles across the overlays.

Arguably the most iconic signature shoe of all time, the Air Jordan 1, gets a look in the game as well. The Eris Rook 1 High comes in leather and suede variations, with a tall ankle collar and laces running almost all the way up. There’s a black-and-white pair that swaps Jordan branding for an Eris basketball graphic on the tongue. You’ve probably got something quite similar in your closet at home.

The Eris Cross Trainers are, well, harder to pin down. Available in several colorways, they have a mesh base and leather overlays. One white-and-gray version gets bright green hits that nod to Nike’s signature “Volt” hue. The simpler construction puts it closer to an older Nike runner, somewhere around MD Runner 2 territory, than a direct Zoom Vomero 5 or V5 Rnr copy. And for those times that tying laces feels like too much work, there are the very appropriately named Eris Basic Slides. The broad branded strap and flat footbed are very Nike Benassi.

There are different versions to consider, too. “Origins” go all-white, while “Elite” options are matte and all-black. So if you‘ve found a silhouette you like, you can still spend another 10 minutes deciding which version works with your trousers. A problem we were hoping to leave outside the game.

It gives you an idea of just how much there is in GTA 6. The older games let you change your clothes, but here you’re choosing between different colorways, materials, and versions of individual shoes. And Eris is only one part of it: There are clothes and accessories that look like takes on Stüssy, Loewe, Chrome Hearts, and Louis Vuitton, too. You could spend a fair bit of time getting dressed before you get anything else done.

We’ve waited this long to play the game. A few more minutes in the sneaker shop before you really get going on missions won’t hurt.

A version of the story originally appeared on British GQ.

This Thanksgiving, step out of your culinary comfort zone and embrace the future of festive feasting. Make a turkey sculpture out of Rice Krispies treats and watch as your holiday transforms from traditional to extraordinary.
