Dua Lipa recently championed the artsy chapeau in a frayed Chanel couture number, while Anya Taylor-Joy opted for a gigantic pink Jacquemus hat that framed her head like a halo. Even winter’s more practical accessories have taken a more eccentric turn: Hunter Schafer has been championing furry, archival Undercover headgear, while Taylor Russell has collaborated with Ilana Blumberg on some particularly fabulous fuzzy hats.

For Wun, the theatricality is very much the point. His fall 2026 couture collection, titled Child's Play, explored childhood and fairytales through a procession of fantastical characters, from Snow White to the Big Bad Wolf. Working with milliner Awon Golding, the designer produced a series of elaborate hats and sculptural headpieces that seemed to defy the laws of gravity.

After seasons of slicked-back buns and minimalist accessories, fashion’s most adventurous dressers are evidently ready for something a little more playful. The message? There’s no such thing as too much drama up top. And as Rosalía has demonstrated, sometimes the best accessories have a life of their own—and take flight.

#6688. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6687. Caramelized Cabbage Pasta

This pasta is the easiest way to cram an entire head of cabbage into one comforting dinner. The secret? Cooking it in butter over a long, relaxed period of time until it softens into a decadent, caramelized tangle. Paired with spaghetti, heavy cream, and some Dijon mustard and lemon zest to brighten everything up, this dish is a celebration of how versatile cabbage can be. Feel free to top your bowl with lots of fresh dill, or leave it unadorned with nothing more than an extra sprinkle of cheese.

Cook 12 oz. spaghetti in a large pot of boiling generously salted water, stirring occasionally, until very al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid. Set aside.

Melt 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pot over high heat. Add 1 large head of green cabbage (about 3 lb.), cored, thinly sliced, and 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring often, until cabbage is very tender and browned in spots, 18–25 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup), 1½ cups heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and reserved pasta to cabbage and toss to coat. If sauce is too thick, add pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time, tossing constantly, until glossy. Taste pasta and season with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with finely chopped dill if desired.

#6686. Exclusive: Shohei Ohtani Just Signed a Historic Deal With New Balance

Shohei Ohtani is used to making history. In addition to his four MLB MVP awards and two World Series rings, the Los Angeles Dodgers two-way great is the first member of the 50/50 club (having racked up 54 home runs and 59 stolen bases during the 2024 season), became the first player to hit three homers and record 10 strikeouts in a single game (which he managed in a 2025 NLCS contest against the Brewers), and earlier this year maintained simultaneous streaks in games on base (48) and innings without an earned run (32 and two-thirds).

Now, the 32-year-old Japanese icon is adding to those accolades with a pioneering endorsement deal, officially extending his relationship with his longtime partner New Balance through to the end of his baseball career. (While a rarefied group of athletes have signed lifetime sponsorship deals—including LeBron James and Cristiano Ronaldo at Nike, and Damian Lillard at Adidas—Ohtani’s new contract appears to be both the first to exclusively cover a star’s playing days and the first of its kind in MLB.)

“There’s a lot of trust,” Ohtani tells me through an interpreter during a sit-down in Boston of his decision to commit to the New England sportswear stalwart for the long haul. “We’ve obviously built friendships, as well. They’ve been able to accommodate my requests, the things I’ve asked for, and, like I said, that takes the involvement of a lot of trust. That relationship has been very, very good and smooth. I had no reservations about extending our relationship.”

Earlier in the day, I shadowed Ohtani at New Balance’s headquarters, where, as part of the agreement, the company is renaming its on-site think tank as the Shohei Ohtani Sports Research Lab. A team of specialists led the Dodgers superstar through a slew of shoes—including his on-field Ohtani 1 model, which will receive new editions in 2027—and then a rack of branded apparel. All of it falls under his Shohei Ohtani Signature Collection, which New Balance launched in 2024 (about a year and a half after the athlete first signed with the company). The collection has grown deliberately and unhurriedly ever since—mirroring his patience in the batter’s box; Ohtani is methodical when it comes to product development and uninterested in rolling out rushed goods with his name slapped on them.

While conducting a kind of footwear postmortem on his 2026 season—which started well, but ended with a rare slump (and left knee and right biceps injuries that kept him from pitching after July 3)—Ohtani noted there’d been some moments of slippage on the heel of his landing foot when pitching. On a printed-out diagram, he used a pencil to sketch ways in which the shoe’s spikes might be slightly reconfigured to find a sweet spot for stability on the mound and speed around the bases. The question of switching footwear between pitching and batting comes up, but Ohtani has not yet done this (and it seems the consensus is to stick with one shoe only).

“I have a lot of direct input into the footwear and apparel,” Ohtani says. “That includes my style, which I like to keep simple, as well as performance-based requests, [like with my] spikes. Some years we make minor changes, and sometimes we’ll make a big change. They understand what I want.”

Ohtani’s apparel line runs across three categories: performance, lifestyle, and fanwear. His custom logo—a striking ink drawing of his figure, designed by the Japanese manga artist Takehiko Inoue—is featured subtly on the bulk of the lineup. “Shohei doesn’t see himself as a glamorous player,” Chris Davis, New Balance brand president and chief marketing officer, tells me. “He sees himself as a gritty, hardworking athlete who wants to get better every day, and his logo reflects this—it has this kind of quiet intensity.”

While some of the future apparel designs boast cool technical features—like detachable, two-in-one, and reversible elements inspired by Ohtani’s two-way play—the man himself is only concerned that his products “fit comfortably and to be easy to wear.” When asked if there’s anyone whose style he likes or is influenced by, Ohtani shrugs. “Honestly, not really. I just like to wear what I like to wear.”

“[Shohei] is very quick and clear with his input,” says Masahiro Uchida, New Balance’s general manager of athlete signature product, who has worked alongside Ohtani for years. “On the performance side, he always prefers softness and a soft hand feel. For the lifestyle side, he prefers clean and simple. He also understands the occasion. He always asks us, ‘Where would I wear this?’” One major goal for Ohtani with his apparel, Uchida adds, is to “support the expansion of baseball culture and show his respect for its heritage. He is a super geek about MLB. He knows so much.”

At 32, the duration of Ohtani’s career—and, now, his New Balance deal—remains an open question. That age can be considered as getting toward the older end in pro baseball, but elite pitchers have a habit of playing well into their 40s—Justin Verlander, for example, just pitched his final season at 43.

Ohtani still plans on being a full two-way player in 2027, with hopes for a Cy Young Award—MLB’s top pitching honor, one of the few laurels he has yet to win—still alive. When the Dodgers’ season ended on October 15, Ohtani told the press that he was “not quite satisfied with how things shaped up on the pitching side.”

What words of advice or motivation does he have, I ask, for the legion of kids hoping to follow in his footsteps? His answer feels like something he might be saying to himself as the next season approaches.

“If you want to become successful, baseball is a sport that takes a lot of repetitive practice,” he says. “You always have to work on your fundamentals. Once you reach a certain level, the sport becomes very, very hard. At that point, you need to remember why you’re playing. Are you playing because you love the sport? If you have that drive, that love for it, then even when it’s tough, you can overcome it.”

#6685. Mario Sorrenti: The Life Behind the Images

During Paris Photo, I visited Mario Sorrenti Diaries, 1991–2000, an exhibition curated by Aaron Stern at LSD, a small gallery on Rue de la Folie Méricourt, in a space that once housed a photographic laboratory. The room was packed, almost overwhelmingly so, and what struck me immediately was the number of young people there. A generation that has grown up with smartphones, accustomed to producing and consuming images at an unprecedented speed, seemed completely fascinated by these handmade books, filled with photographs, Polaroids, contact sheets, handwritten notes, drawings and fragments of a life lived more than thirty years ago.

I found myself wondering what drew them so strongly to these objects. Was it nostalgia for a time they had never experienced? A fascination with the physicality of photography, with the idea that images once existed as tangible things, objects to be touched, collected, cut, pasted and preserved? Or perhaps something more profound: a longing for authenticity, for the traces of real experiences, for a relationship with images that feels increasingly distant from the way we encounter them today?

The more I looked at Mario's diaries, the more I felt that the answer lay somewhere in that last possibility.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

Mario Sorrenti is one of the defining photographers of his generation, an artist whose work has profoundly influenced the visual language of fashion photography since the early 1990s. His contribution to Vogue Italia alone is extraordinary. Over the years, he has created an extensive body of editorials that remain part of the magazine's visual history, images that helped shape not only the aesthetics of fashion but also the way fashion could communicate desire, intimacy and emotion.

His signature is unmistakable, yet it cannot be reduced to a particular technique or aesthetic formula. There is the extraordinary sensitivity with which he approaches light, whether soft and natural or dramatic and carefully controlled. There is his attention to skin, texture and the physical presence of the body, his ability to move between the immediacy of a seemingly spontaneous photograph and the formal sophistication of an elaborately constructed image.

Above all, there is his particular way of representing sensuality.

Fashion photography has always had a complex relationship with desire, and Mario certainly wasn't the first photographer to explore intimacy or eroticism. But he brought something distinctly his own to that tradition. In his photographs, sensuality never feels imposed on the subject. It seems to emerge from the relationship between the photographer and the person in front of his camera. Even when an image is provocative, there is often a tenderness, a vulnerability, an emotional proximity that prevents it from becoming merely an exercise in seduction.

Perhaps the most famous example remains his photographs of Kate Moss, who was his girlfriend at the time, particularly the images that led to the iconic Calvin Klein Obsession campaign in 1993. Their extraordinary power came not simply from Kate's beauty or Mario's photographic talent, but from the genuine intimacy of their relationship. These were not images in which intimacy was staged for the camera. They emerged from an existing emotional connection, from a shared life, before becoming part of the collective visual memory of an era.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

And this is where the exhibition in Paris becomes especially revealing.Rather than presenting the celebrated photographs that established Mario's reputation, it turns its attention to the world from which those images emerged.

The five diaries, spanning the years between 1991 and 2000, bring together photographs, contact sheets, handwritten notes, drawings and fragments of everyday life. For the exhibition, Mario reproduced the pages of his original journals using color Xerox machines, then reassembled and bound them by hand. These are not conventional photographic books, nor simply archival documents. They occupy a fascinating territory between memory, artistic experimentation and the physical act of making.

There are portraits, faces, bodies, moments of everyday life, images of friends and lovers, familiar figures from the fashion world, and deeply personal traces of the people who surrounded him. There are handwritten words, repetitions, experiments, sequences of images that seem to follow the associative logic of memory rather than the conventions of photographic editing.

What makes this particularly fascinating is that Mario's diaries were not simply something he created alongside his photographic career. They were fundamental to its development. He began taking pictures in New York in the late 1980s, teaching himself photography while documenting the world around him, even building a darkroom in his mother's laundry room. It was precisely these personal diaries that, when he showed them to Calvin Klein in 1993, inspired the iconic Obsession campaign.

The boundary between personal work and commissioned photography was never as clear as we might imagine. For many great photographers, this distinction becomes almost meaningless. It is precisely their personal vision, shaped by experiences, relationships and an ongoing process of exploration, that makes their work immediately recognizable, regardless of the context in which it is created. At its highest level, fashion photography is no longer simply in the service of a product, but becomes a space for genuine artistic exploration.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

The photographs are inseparable from the people Mario loved, the places he inhabited and the cultural atmosphere that shaped him. What emerges is not only the development of a photographic language but the formation of a sensibility.

I was particularly touched by this because I lived in New York during those same years. Mario and I belong to the same generation, and although our experiences were our own, we inhabited the same city, at the same moment, within a cultural world that was undergoing an extraordinary transformation.

New York in the 1990s was a place of intense creative exchange, where fashion, photography, music, art and nightlife constantly intersected. There was a sense of freedom, experimentation and possibility, but also a rawness, an urgency, a willingness to take risks and to blur the boundaries between one's personal life and creative work.

Looking through Mario's diaries, I recognized something of that world. Not necessarily the same people or the same experiences, but the atmosphere, the energy, the particular feeling of being young in a city where life and creativity seemed impossible to separate.

There is also the extraordinary family Mario comes from, a remarkable constellation of creative talent. His mother, Francesca Sorrenti, a woman of exceptional talent and an enormously influential figure in the worlds of fashion and image-making; his sister Vanina, an extraordinarily gifted photographer in her own right; and his younger brother Davide, who died tragically young in 1997, an exceptional photographer whose work captured the spirit of a generation with rare sensitivity and immediacy.

In this family, photography has never been simply a profession. It has been a shared language, a way of relating to one another and to the world. Perhaps this helps explain why Mario's work feels so deeply personal, even when it is created within the highly sophisticated machinery of the fashion industry.

Davide's presence in the diaries is particularly poignant. Knowing his story, these images become more than fragments of a shared youth. They are traces of a relationship, of love, of loss, of a world that no longer exists except through the images that remain.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris

And this brings us back to something fundamental about photography: its extraordinary relationship with time.

A photograph preserves a moment while simultaneously reminding us that the moment is gone. But in Mario's diaries, this relationship becomes even more complex. Photographs are placed alongside words, drawings, other photographs, fragments of thought. They are revisited, rearranged, reproduced and transformed. Memory becomes an active creative process rather than a passive act of preservation.

The use of Xerox is especially interesting in this respect. Reproduction here is not simply a means of copying an original. It becomes part of the artistic language itself. The texture, the imperfections, the altered colors, the materiality of the pages all contribute to the emotional experience of the work. The diaries remind us that photographs have a physical existence, and that the way we handle, sequence and preserve them can be as meaningful as the images themselves.

In an era when billions of photographs circulate through our screens, when images are increasingly detached from physical objects and, with artificial intelligence, can even be generated without any corresponding lived experience, this feels particularly significant.

We photograph everything, store everything, share everything. Yet how often do we return to those images and give them the attention necessary to become part of our memory? Mario's diaries speak instead of time spent looking, selecting, arranging, touching and remembering: the physical labor of creating meaning from the fragments of one's existence.

And perhaps this is why that small gallery in Paris was so crowded with young people.

I don't think their fascination was simply nostalgic. Nostalgia implies a desire to return to something we have lost, but many of those visitors had never known the world these diaries describe. Perhaps what they were responding to was something more immediate and universal: the evidence of a real life, with all its beauty, contradictions, intimacy and imperfections.

We often discuss the signature of a photographer in terms of light, composition, color or technique. But perhaps the most distinctive element of an artist's visual language lies somewhere deeper, in the particular way they have experienced the world. Before an image becomes iconic, before it enters the history of photography or the collective imagination, it begins with someone looking at something, or someone, and feeling compelled to remember.

Mario Sorrenti Diaries, 1991–2000, curated by Aaron Stern, is on view at LSD, 20 Rue de la Folie Méricourt, Paris, from November 12 to December 10, 2026.

#6683. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6682. Red-Wine-Braised Short Ribs

These red-wine-braised short ribs have fans. “This has been my go-to recipe for short ribs for as long as I can remember,” says one commenter. “It never fails.” It’s the kind of special-occasion dish you make once and return to forever.

Flavor builds in layers: The bone-in beef is browned, then the onions, carrots, and celery cook in its drippings. A full bottle of dry red wine reduces by half before the broth goes in; a whole head of garlic and plenty of fresh herbs round out the braise. After that, a few hours in the oven turn the meat fall-off-the-bone tender.

Even better: You can make the ribs a day ahead, leaving little to do before dinner but reheat them. Serve over mashed potatoes, soft polenta, or wide egg noodles to soak up every drop of the rich sauce.

Look for meaty, bone-in English-cut short ribs, with a single rib bone beneath each piece of meat. Ask your butcher to cut them crosswise into 2" lengths—you’re not expected to saw through the bones at home. Avoid the thin strips sold for grilling.

What’s the best wine for braised short ribs?

Choose a dry red wine you’d enjoy drinking. Cabernet Sauvignon is the recipe’s first choice, but Merlot or a Rhône-style red also fits the bill. There’s no need to splurge; save your special bottle for the table.

For the smooth sauce intended here, yes. The vegetables flavor the braising liquid, and straining removes them along with the herb stems, bay leaves, and garlic skins.

For a more rustic approach, pluck out the herbs and garlic skins (leave the cloves behind) and use an immersion blender to purée the cooked vegetables into the sauce.

Start checking after 2 hours in the oven. A fork should slide into the meat easily, and a gentle twist should pull it apart. If the meat still resists, keep braising. The listed cooking time is a guide, not a hard stop.

Can I make these short ribs ahead, and how should I reheat them?

Yes. Finish cooking the ribs and strain the sauce, then refrigerate the ribs with their sauce in shallow containers within 2 hours of cooking. The next day, lift off the hardened fat. Transfer the ribs and sauce to an ovenproof pot or baking dish, cover, and reheat in a 350° oven until hot throughout—the meat should reach 165° in the center.

Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app

Try this recipe with this expert pick from the Bon Appétit Wine Shop.

Staub Enameled Cast Iron Round Dutch Oven 7-Qt.

Preheat oven to 350°. Season 5 lb. bone-in beef short ribs, cut crosswise into 2" pieces by your butcher, with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Working in 2 batches, cook short ribs, turning occasionally, until browned on all sides, about 8 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate. Pour off all but 3 Tbsp. drippings from pot.

Cook 3 medium onions, chopped, 3 medium carrots, peeled, chopped, and 2 celery stalks, chopped, in same pot over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onions are browned, about 5 minutes. Add 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until combined and deep red, 2–3 minutes.

Stir in one 750-ml bottle dry red wine (preferably Cabernet Sauvignon), then add short ribs along with any juices that have accumulated on the plate. Bring to a boil; reduce heat to medium and simmer until wine is reduced by half, about 25 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, halved crosswise, 10 sprigs parsley, 8 sprigs thyme, 4 sprigs oregano, 2 sprigs rosemary, and 2 fresh or dried bay leaves; stir in 4 cups low-sodium beef broth. Bring to a boil, cover, and transfer pot to oven. Braise until short ribs are tender, 2–2½ hours.

Uncover pot and transfer short ribs to a platter. Strain sauce through a fine-mesh sieve into a heatproof measuring glass; spoon fat from surface and discard. Season sauce with salt and pepper. Arrange ribs in shallow bowls, over mashed potatoes if desired, and spoon sauce over.

As your character gets stronger, their avatar transforms accordingly, developing more defined muscles, a six-pack, and even a chiseled face. Neglecting your fitness and overeating (a real thing you can do in the game) has an alternate effect as your player visibly gains weight and adopts a “dad bod.”

But don’t think that just because it’s all on a screen that you won’t walk away from a session with a little back pain, so maybe schedule a few breaks in between. You could even build a home gym of your own like Jason’s—it’s already got one fitness expert’s approval.

#6680. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

#6678. How to Survive Politics Talk at Thanksgiving (Without Losing Your Mind)

Thanksgiving is almost upon us, and given that we’re fresh off a midterms blue wave in the US, it’s probably not realistic to expect the holiday to be totally free of political drama. (Unless every member of your family is magically politically aligned on every issue, but when has that ever happened?)

While tapping out of politics talk entirely doesn’t feel like an option in 2026, it feels equally dismal to simply accept a tense or outright hostile environment during what should be a joyful and grateful time of year. Personally, I can vouch for the strategy of finding small political-adjacent moments to unite over, even if they feel frivolous—for example, your DSA-member sister and your establishment-Democrat mom may not align on all of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s policies, but you can probably get them both to agree that watching him personally shovel New Yorkers’ snow last winter was adorable.

For some expert guidance on this issue, Vogue spoke to Dr. Audra Nuru, a professor of communication and family studies at the University of St. Thomas in St. Paul, Minnesota, about how to engage loved ones with differing views in a productive way (and, just as importantly, how to set boundaries when it feels like engagement is no longer good for you and your mental health). Find her thoughts—and some sample scripts she's provided for different conversations—below.

Vogue: How do you recommend preparing for an event or gathering that might include viewpoints you disagree with or find harmful?

Dr. Audra Nuru: It’s true that those kinds of encounters can benefit from a bit of preparation. I like to think of it like packing for a trip to a new and unfamiliar place—you want to be prepared for the expected, but also pack with an open mind for the unexpected. So, before heading into that event, take some time to reflect on what topics might feel a bit sensitive for you, almost like checking the weather forecast, so you can pack accordingly. Remember, everyone is coming to the table with their own unique experiences and perspectives. Embrace those differences with curiosity and kindness. And of course, it’s always wise to set healthy boundaries—that’s like having a good map and a reliable guide to help you navigate any unfamiliar territory.

Is there a subtle, useful way to redirect a political conversation that's starting to feel upsetting?

First and foremost, prioritize the relationship. Remember that the person you’re talking to matters more than proving a point. Ask yourself, “How can I express my views while still showing respect and valuing this person?” Part of showing respect is acknowledging that you may have different perspectives. If a conversation starts to feel a little uncomfortable, try gently saying something like, “I hear you, and I hold a different perspective.” This lets the other person know you’re listening and that their views matter, even if you don’t agree.

Secondly, listen with your heart, not just your head. Truly try to understand where they’re coming from, even if you disagree. What experiences have shaped their beliefs? What emotions are they expressing? And remember, even when it’s tough, try to see things from their perspective. Stepping into another’s shoes, even for a moment, can foster understanding and empathy.

Third, look for points of connection. Even in the midst of disagreement, there’s often some shared experiences or common ground to connect on. It can also be valuable to sense when a conversation needs a pause. If things are starting to feel tense, it’s completely fine to suggest taking a break or shifting to a different topic. Ultimately, navigating difficult conversations with respect is about how we connect, even when we disagree. It’s about building bridges of understanding by making space for different perspectives.

What’s a respectful yet firm way to let someone know their comments have crossed a line?

Using “I” language is such a powerful tool for navigating difficult conversations. Instead of pointing fingers, “I” language lets us shift the focus to our own experience. Imagine saying something like, “I felt uncomfortable when I heard that comment.” It’s honest, it’s respectful, and it avoids making the other person feel attacked. When we own our feelings, it invites the other person to do the same. It creates this space for empathy and understanding, even when we might disagree.

#6676. 31 Thanksgiving Dinner Alternatives to Turkey

Honestly, anything can make for an alternative Thanksgiving dinner. It’s your house, your rules. Our only suggestion: Make it festive, fun, and at least a little decadent.

A classic Thanksgiving menu is all well and good, but one of our colleagues swears by serving nachos on the fourth Thursday of every November. If a big bloomin’ bird just isn’t ca-caw-caw-calling your name this year, serve a whole roast fish, pork tenderloin with sour-sweet cherry sauce, or a flaky carrot Wellington instead.

Or go completely rogue with lobster pasta or a big pot of chili. You can do that. Below, find vegetarian centerpieces, celebratory roasts, chicken dinners, and seafood mains for a Thanksgiving that looks a little different. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie can stay.

Can carrots really count as a main course? They can when they’re roasted, glazed, and tucked into puff pastry with goat cheese, Gruyère, and walnuts. This Wellington feeds 8 to 10.

Red wine, browned mushrooms, pearl onions, and carrots give this meatless braise plenty of heft. Ladle it over mashed potatoes for a vegetarian anchor to your Thanksgiving menu.

Ruffled savoy cabbage, melty cheese, and a buttery cream cheese crust make this free-form tart worthy of the holiday table. Cut generous wedges for dinner and stick with savoy: Ordinary green cabbage won’t work here.

A make-ahead casserole, like this pumpkin-infused strata scented with nutmeg and herbs and balanced by sharp cheddar, is just what your holiday schedule needs. Assemble it the night before; bake it on Thanksgiving.

Turkey isn’t the only holiday cooking project worth clearing the counter for. Delicate homemade crepes are rolled around ricotta, mozzarella, and Parmesan, then baked in marinara. Make the batter and filling a day ahead to split up the work.

Kale, pinto beans, and charred poblanos make these cheesy enchiladas a satisfying holiday main for four to six. Get a head start by making the charred salsa verde up to three days ahead.

This autumnal risotto works as a standalone dinner or alongside your favorite Thanksgiving sides. Set the table with shallow bowls and pick a fall salad full of color and crunch to balance the buttery rice.

British beef Wellington meets Cantonese barbecue-style pork in Peter Som’s pastry-wrapped centerpiece. A shiitake mushroom filling and gravy made from the marinade complete the picture; assemble the Wellington a day ahead.

These impossibly tender short ribs are begging to be served with mashed potatoes and buttery milk buns with garlic butter. Give them what they want—and give yourself a head start by braising the ribs the day before Thanksgiving.

Brisket more your speed? Try our Brisket Bourguignon →

Turkey skin has competition. Tender pork belly, crisp crackling, and a hard cider pan sauce make a persuasive case for skipping the bird. Pass the chile vinegar to cut through the richness; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Ayesha Curry’s spice-crusted prime rib takes its cues from her mother’s braised oxtails, with habanero crema on the side. Prefer a simpler garlic-and-rosemary approach? Try this Low-and-Slow Rib Roast.

For a roast-and-sides Thanksgiving without the turkey, garlic-and-rosemary-rubbed beef tenderloin makes an excellent centerpiece. Rosemary butter dresses the sliced roast, while tangy horseradish yogurt gives everyone something to swipe their next bite through.

Toasted rice, fried onions, and garlic form a dark, peppery crust on this slow-braised pork shoulder. Set out the big platter and pass the coconut-vinegar pan sauce; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Maybe save the brown sugar-glazed ham for Christmas? This whole leg of lamb makes for a centerpiece that’s just as showstopping. And, like ham and turkey, leftover lamb can be deliciously repurposed in sandwiches.

A platter of sliced pork tenderloin with glossy cherries and browned shallots has plenty of holiday presence without a long roast. Honey and red wine vinegar give the sauce its sweet-sour bite, and frozen cherries are welcome here.

If you’re going to make tamales, it’s a good idea to make a lot of them. Better yet, turn the process into a party, with everyone spreading masa and folding corn husks around the red chile pork filling.

This pasta packs a whole spectrum of holiday flavors into each bite, with crumbles of Italian sausage, shreds of brussels sprouts, and toasted pecans. Streamlining dinner into one dish leaves you more time for Thanksgiving pies.

For some people, spending all Thanksgiving in the kitchen sounds like a good time. For everyone else, there’s this beef-and-bean chili. A can of pumpkin purée thickens the broth, keeping things seasonal without calling for a single roasting pan.

Give homemade fried chicken an even more festive angle with sage and thyme in the dredge and cranberry-mustard sauce for dipping. Start the buttermilk marinade the day before.

This whole roast duck comes with a built-in Thanksgiving side: The duck fat drippings go into basmati rice that cooks while the bird rests. Plan for an overnight dry brine before the glossy pomegranate-honey glaze gets its moment.

Cooking for a smaller crowd? This skillet delivers the stuffing and the bird—chicken thighs, in this case—in one tidy package. Rendered chicken fat enriches the boxed stuffing mix, with dried cranberries and lemon zest brightening things up.

Two diminutive birds make a festive roast for four. A fiery guajillo chile, ginger, and vinegar marinade flavors both the hens and the potatoes beneath them, so the platter arrives with its own very good side.

You just need to make green beans, because this Thanksgiving main is already a two-in-one: Thinly sliced potatoes cook beneath a whole chicken, catching its drippings and crisping around the edges in the same cast-iron skillet.

If your Thanksgiving table could use a little red sauce (and spice), skip the whole bird in favor of this take on chicken parm. Gochujang and gochugaru bring the heat; melted mozzarella keeps things gloriously gooey.

José Andrés turns chicken wings and a colorful assortment of vegetables into a grand centerpiece, with saffron and smoked paprika flavoring the rice. You’ll need a 15" paella pan or comparably sized two-handled cast-iron or cast-aluminum pan.

There’s nothing like pasta to stretch a spendy ingredient (hello, lobster). Serve with a big crunchy salad with Italian dressing and garlic confit toast that diners can pass around for Thanksgiving party vibes.

Presenting a whole fish at the holiday table is wildly celebratory, even when you’re cooking for just two or three. Bring out lettuce wraps, kimchi, rice, and ssamjang so everyone can build each bite a little differently.

A large roasted salmon fillet looks right at home on a holiday platter, especially under a crunchy, garlicky nut salsa. Make the salsa up to four days ahead, then roast the fish when it’s time for dinner.

The stuffing doesn’t have to be a side. Here, crushed boxed stuffing mix joins Parmesan, lemon zest, and parsley in a crisp crust for mustard-coated white fish. Dinner lands on the table in 25 minutes.

This dark, glossy coconut caramel—savory with fish sauce and garlic, sharp with pickled jalapeño brine—turns pan-seared salmon into a holiday-worthy main. Serve with rice to catch every last bit of sauce.

Like many of the best Thanksgiving dishes, this one starts with a good stock. Carla Hall builds a fennel potlikker with celery, onions, and Pernod before layering those flavors into a hearty bowl of shrimp and grits.

#6675. Nigella Lawson’s Best Baking Advice Of All Time

There are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson. If she told me to put sardines in a birthday cake, I’d believe her. That’s just the kind of culinary authority you earn after nearly three decades of making us hungry through the TV screen. The cookbook author and television personality is now dishing out advice on The Great British Baking Show—she made her debut as a GBBS judge in September—but it’s just a small window into her extensive wisdom.

From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.

Cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does. “I think every recipe has to be as precise as possible,” Lawson told Vogue in 2018. “Baking, you have to be really precise. If you’re cooking and it suggests 2 to 3 carrots, it doesn’t really matter because they can be different sizes. It’s not going to alter the taste.”

So, you’ve never really baked before. It’s okay to start small! A three-tier chantilly cake your first day in the kitchen probably isn’t your best bet. “It’s important to go for a simple recipe. Read through the recipe to make sure you understand everything that’s being told to you at the time,” she said. “Look for a recipe that gives you an indication of what to do at each stage. This is what I always say to people: remind yourself you’re not running a restaurant.”

If you’ve been making your chocolate cake with milk, here’s your sign to stop. Lawson suggests swapping the dairy for hot or boiling water instead to “bloom” the cocoa, dissolve the sugar, and loosen the batter. The result? A crazy moist crumb!

Instead of using plain water when baking bread, Lawson suggests swapping it out for leftover pasta or potato water. “It will help the bread’s texture and rise,” she wrote on X in 2020. “Taste it before adding, though. If very salty, dilute it with fresh water and, obviously, leave any salt in the recipe out.”

It might sound weird, but Lawson swears by cream of tartar for fluffier, softer scones. “These are the best [ones] I’ve ever eaten, which is quite how it should be since they emanate from one of those old-fashioned cooks who starts a batch the minute the doorbell rings at teatime,” she wrote on her website in 2017. “Yes, I know they look as if they’ve got cellulite—it’s the cream of tartar, which is also why, despite their apparent solidity, they have that dreamy lightness.”

Lawson’s genius baking hack? DIY self-rising flour. “Nigella tends not to use self-raising flour in her more recent books as she doesn’t bother to keep both plain (all-purpose) and self-raising flour,” her site reads. “Partly because keeping just one type of flour saves on storage space, and partly because if you don’t use self-raising flour regularly, then it will lose its raising power over time.”

Instead, simply add 2 teaspoons of baking powder for each cup of plain flour. Sift the flour and baking powder together into a bowl before using (and make sure the baking powder is fully integrated), and you’re golden!

We’re all a little extra busy around the holidays, so if you’re planning a dinner party or holiday get-together, it’s okay to make shortcuts. Even Lawson says not everything has to be baked from scratch.

“I have a bit of a weakness for this sort of cake, which is essentially an assembly-job number, a construction of alternate layers of a rich, boozy cream and some store-bought sponge or other,” she told the BBC in 2023 about one of her favorite holiday desserts. “Here the layers comprise a confection of cream and mascarpone, seasonally spiked with Advocaat, full of crystallized ginger, figs and nuts, and that essential component of Christmas: gingerbread.”

Even Lawson admits: “just the words ‘uniformity of size and shape’ make [her] quake.” Hello, crazy foreshadowing for her future on GBBS.

“I am not in the slightest bit insecure about what I can bake, and I’m so very happy doing it, but shop-bought perfection is way beyond me,” she said in a 2014 interview with The Guardian. “But I’m perfectly content with that, and with the ramshackle homemade-ness of my creations.” If that’s good enough for Nigella, it’s good enough for me!

#6674. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6673. Jennifer Lopez Isn’t Beating the Elizabeth Taylor Allegations

Jennifer Lopez has more than a little in common with Elizabeth Taylor. Both have lived out their love lives in the glare of the public eye—comparisons between the two have only intensified since J Lo’s fourth divorce, with Taylor famously having walked down the aisle eight times—and both know the power of an extravagant outfit.

For the Los Angeles premiere of her concert film The JLo Show on Thursday night, Lopez channeled old Hollywood glamour in a Dolce & Gabbana lace gown and an elaborately embroidered opera coat. But it was her jewelry that would really have caught Elizabeth Taylor’s eye: a white-gold Alta Gioielleria Sicilia necklace featuring a whopping 100.10-carat yellow diamond, with matching earrings.

Taylor’s own huge diamond, ruby, and gold archive have been called upon a’plenty: Margot Robbie wore Taylor’s iconic heart-shaped Taj Mahal diamond set in a Cartier necklace while promoting Wuthering Heights, and Kim Kardashian walked the Balenciaga fall 2025 couture show in Paris wearing diamond pendant earrings once worn by Taylor, on loan from jeweler-to-the-stars Lorraine Schwartz. Taylor Swift remains the most ardent modern collector.

Elizabeth Taylor knew a thing or two about a statement jewel. A passionate collector, her jewelry box included a Bvlgari ring featuring a 2.62-carat yellow diamond—a 30th-birthday gift from her fourth husband, Eddie Fisher—and a yellow diamond bracelet gifted to her by Michael Jackson, which fetched £119,700 at auction in 2025. Jennifer Lopez might have a few marriages to go before she catches up with Taylor, but in the jewelry stakes? She’s giving her a run for her money.

#6672. 14 Best Barn Coats for Men in 2026, According to GQ Editors

The best barn coats for men are a close cousin of the chore jacket—similar in spirit, but built tougher. They’re heartier, heavier, better insulated, and usually more water-resistant. Where the chore jacket belonged to the factory floor, the barn coat was made for the fields: a layer you could shrug on to tackle chores outdoors.

But ever since the ’80s and ’90s, the barn coat has been finding a new audience of urbanites who understand its utility, even on mean city streets. Today, alongside the waxy Barbour zip-ups and dad-approved L.L. Bean riffs, a ton of capital-F fashion labels—The Row, Auralee, Prada—have been herding the barn coat back into the center of the style conversation.

Reading to buy your first barn coat? Make sure it’s cut with enough room to comfortably slip a sweater beneath it, and that its craftsmanship ensures it’ll remain a reliable rotation beater for years to come. The former, of course, might demand some trial and error on your end, but the latter is exactly where we come in. These are the absolute best barn coats for men on the market right now, from the genre-defining joints you already know to the sleeper-hit versions you probably don’t.

Deep, easily accessed pockets? A warm corduroy collar? A charming plaid lining? This jacket from J.Crew is, quite simply, the platonic ideal of a barn coat. It has all the details dialed in, built upon a sturdy, 100% cotton washed canvas body that will only soften and feel more like your own in time. Originally launched over 40 years ago, there’s a reason J.Crew is still able to sell it four decades later. And we didn’t even mention the hook on the back, so you can hang this up with ease as soon as you enter your bustling, warm, overcrowded local bar. It’s the little things.

I should disclose up front that I’m a bit of an OrSlow obsessive. I own more from the brand than I’ll ever admit publicly or privately and doubt that I’ve ever been unaware of something it’s produced, but this is because no brand has more consistently lived-up to pre-purchase expectations in my illustrious shopping career, and the only things that see the light of day are things that are absolutely dialed. And this jacket is dialed, folks. Made in Japan from start to finish, it has the kind of cut that can handle a Joey Tribbiani-esque volume of layers, is made from a cotton canvas fabric that will look unreal in half a decade, and the type of construction that other brands show factories when they’re trying to describe what they’re looking for.

We couldn’t round out a piece on barn coats without a nod to L.L. Bean, one of the OGs of the style. A century ago, Bean launched a rugged duck-hunting coat that slowly shifted into a catch-all field jacket—the ancestor of the one they’re still selling today. It’s made from hefty, water-resistant canvas, with a sewn-in lining, five roomy pockets, underarm gussets, and bi-swing shoulders so you can actually move in it. And like many things Bean, the sizing is inclusive, there’s even a “Tall” option for the vertically gifted among us.

The Real McCoy’s is known for painstakingly recreating vintage garments—the Abercrombie set that Hunter S. Thompson made famous is an all-timer—so you can bank on the fact that this barn jacket has all the proper credentials. If you are dubious, however, know that it’s made out of a damn-near-bulletproof cotton canvas fabric, is fully lined with twill to trap some heat when things get chilly, has a perfect hit of corduroy at the collar and comes equipped with one of the sickest pocket configurations you’ll ever see in the genre. It’s hard to call anything “perfect,” but I feel comfortable saying that this is an ideal barn jacket, and would be hard to beat against any rubric.

What’s all this, then—a Barbour as a barn coat? The Beaufort isn’t cut from the same stiff American canvas, but the brief is identical: a country jacket for tramping through fields, feeding the chickens, or—let’s be honest—making it to the pub. King Charles even reinstated the brand’s Royal Warrant last year (he is the Menswear King, after all). Built long before DWR and Gore-Tex, its waxed cotton shrugs off rain, the oversize corduroy collar blocks the wind, and you can zip in liners or snap on a hood if you feel like accessorizing. Best detail? The little hand-warmer pockets perched above the main ones—perfect for thawing fingers after a day of grouse shooting or a lap of the Lower East Side. Just remember: it will need the occasional re-waxing, but that’s all part of the fun.

If you're getting hung up on the idea of a barn jacket that’s implicitly unqualified to do barn jacket work, this isn’t going to be the one for you. But you if think that the barn jacket can be both a highly-functional, historically-revered workwear staple AND that it’s a brilliant canvas on which the most tasteful among us can mess around a little, this one from the maniacs (complimentary) at Auralee is hypnotic. The outer is made from a cotton moleskin—which is like flannel’s heavyweight cousin, for those unfamiliar—that’s been unevenly garment-dyed to look like it’s endured thousands of miles on a tractor. Meanwhile, the pockets are flawless, the zipped placket comes outfitted with a buttoned storm flap, and the whole thing is garnished with a detachable shearling collar, just in case you thought they spared a single expense along the way.

Knickerbocker is known for tasteful pieces that can help you rebuild an entire wardrobe, and that includes this faithful homage to vintage fly-fishing wading jackets commonly worn in the jacket’s namesake upstate region. The Portuguese canvas and rounded collar stand out among other jackets on our list, and the gusseted shoulders allow for a wide range of movement on and off the river.

First off, don't fear the red colorway. It's just as easy to wear as any other fall-adjacent color and it stands out roughly twice as much, which is kind of the dream ratio for eye-catching jackets. Also, it's just a damn-good barn coat, with deep ol' hand pockets, a wind-stopping corduroy collar and endless layering potential.

This is absolutely a barn jacket. All the hallmarks are there, from the corduroy collar (more on that later) to the generous pocket situation and layout. But it's also one of the most stunning corduroy jackets on the market due to one of the most breathtaking corduroys you will ever see. And if you ever were wondering, why don't they make the whole jacket out of the collar, they do.

Filson's classic Barn-adjacent coat is an undeniable giant in the space—big ol' stow pockets, corduroy collar, canvas outer—but the insulated iteration is every bit as easy to wear and twice as warm, without adding much bulk at all.

Think of this TS joint as the ultimate "what if." Like, what if, instead of a classic canvas outer there was a super soft, ultra sturdy, almost flannel-like flocked denim? And instead of corduroy, TS threw in a leather collar? Because across the board, they decided to find out.

Much like the Auralee number up top, this isn't the kind of barn jacket that you'd be wearing to bale hay, but there's only a select few among us doing that anyways. You can, however, wear the living hell out of this all winter long, because not only does it layer beautifully, it has the requisite storage, showstopping potential and only gets better with age. Is it practical? That's not the point.

Levi’s takes a no-nonsense swing at the barn jacket—exactly what you’d expect from them. You get a sturdy shell, a quilted lining that brings just the right amount of warmth, and two generous front pockets. Sure, it skips the classic hand-warmer pockets, but at a price this good, you can afford to overlook a detail or two.

This is one of the most affordable options on this list, but you're not leaving a ton on the table if this is your prefered route. The outer is a waxed organic cotton that will hold up well against all forms of precipitation, there's a full flannel lining and the collar even buttons into a stand, to really keep things insulated.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6670. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.
